findings.explanation: The new `delete` handler fetches a `NotificationSettingOption` by `notification_option_id` alone, without verifying that the fetched record belongs to the authenticated `user` passed in from `UserEndpoint.convert_args`. The `UserPermission.has_object_permission` check (lines 15-26 of `src/sentry/api/bases/user.py`) only validates that the requesting user matches the `user_id` URL parameter — it performs no check on the child resource. Because the `notification_option_id` is a separate URL parameter that is never cross-referenced against `option.user_id == user.id`, any authenticated user who knows (or can guess) any `notification_option_id` can delete a notification setting belonging to a different user.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `user_id` filter to the database lookup so that the fetched option is guaranteed to belong to the authenticated user: `NotificationSettingOption.objects.get(id=notification_option_id, user_id=user.id)`. This ensures that supplying a valid `notification_option_id` that belongs to a different user results in a 404 rather than an unauthorized deletion.

findings.explanation: The PUT handler at user_notification_providers.py:72-79 uses `scope_identifier` directly from user-supplied request data as a lookup key in `update_or_create`. When `scope_type` is TEAM or ORGANIZATION, `scope_identifier` is an arbitrary integer (team ID or org ID) submitted by the requester. The new `UserNotificationSettingsProvidersDetailsSerializer.validate_scope_type` (validators.py:66-74) only validates that the scope_type string is one of the allowed enum values; it does NOT verify that the acting user is actually a member of the team or organization identified by `scope_identifier`. The base validator `validate_scope` (api/validators/notifications.py:43-59) performed a user-ownership check for USER scope, but no equivalent membership check existed for TEAM/ORGANIZATION scope there either — however, that path was previously used only in contexts that enforced org/team membership through separate endpoint permissions. This new endpoint inherits only `UserEndpoint`/`UserPermission` (user.py:14-26), which solely checks that `request.user.id == user.id`. A user can therefore supply any arbitrary team or organization ID as `scope_identifier` and create/update notification provider settings scoped to teams or organizations they do not belong to.

findings.suggested_fix: When `scope_type` is TEAM or ORGANIZATION, validate that the authenticated user (`request.user`) is actually a member of the team or organization identified by `scope_identifier` before performing `update_or_create`. For USER scope, enforce that `scope_identifier` equals the acting user's own ID. This check should be added either in `validate_scope_type`/a cross-field `validate()` method on `UserNotificationSettingsProvidersDetailsSerializer`, or in the `put` view handler itself, querying `OrganizationMember` or `OrganizationMemberTeam` to verify membership.

findings.explanation: The DELETE endpoint `UserNotificationOptionsDetailEndpoint.delete()` fetches a `NotificationSettingOption` by `notification_option_id` alone without verifying that the option belongs to the authenticated user. The `UserEndpoint.convert_args` in `user.py` resolves and permission-checks the `user` object (lines 65-76), but the endpoint's delete handler only queries `NotificationSettingOption.objects.get(id=notification_option_id)` without filtering by `user_id=user.id`. This means any authenticated user can delete any other user's notification option by supplying its numeric ID. The new test suite (`test_user_notification_options_details.py`) only tests the authenticated user deleting their own option and a missing ID returning 404 — it never tests cross-user deletion, so this IDOR flaw is completely uncovered and newly introduced by the PR.
